title: How much time is repetitive work costing your business?
description: Repeated data entry and routine handoffs can quietly fill a workweek. Here is what small-business surveys tell us, and how to find a sensible starting point for automation in your own business.
body:
A customer sends in a request. Someone copies the details into a spreadsheet, adds them to another system, and sends a message to the person who needs to act on it.

Each step might take only a few minutes. Repeat that process throughout the week, and it becomes a regular part of someone's job. For a small business, those minutes compete with serving customers, preparing estimates, and getting home on time.

Before buying another tool, it is worth asking a practical question: where are we doing the same work more than once?

## What the numbers tell us

In a survey published by Zapier in September 2026, 55% of respondents said they had repetitive manual tasks or processes they had considered automating but had not yet automated. The survey covered 508 U.S. owners and operators of businesses with fewer than 500 employees. [Zapier survey](https://zapier.com/blog/ai-governance-for-small-teams/)

The time involved can be substantial. In its 2024 survey of 630 U.S. owners and executives at businesses with 10–99 employees, Intuit QuickBooks reported 25 hours per week per business spent on manual data entry or reconciling information across apps. Its methodology identifies its averages as weighted medians. This is a business-wide benchmark, not time lost by each employee or a measure of how much automation would save. [Intuit QuickBooks survey](https://erp.intuit.com/blog/research/business-solutions-survey-2024/)

There is also evidence of perceived benefits. Among automation users in that 2026 Zapier survey, 43% reported freeing up time for higher-value work. That means 43% of those users reported a benefit, not that they saved 43% of their working hours. [Zapier survey](https://zapier.com/blog/ai-governance-for-small-teams/)

Both studies were commissioned by software vendors and rely on respondents' reports. They are useful context, not a prediction for your business. Some administration is necessary, and not every manual task should be automated.

## Look for the repeatable steps

Consider a few hypothetical examples:

- Customer intake: A service business receives a completed form. Instead of retyping the same details, a workflow could create an internal record and assign someone to review it.
- Job handoffs: When a team marks a job ready for scheduling, a workflow could notify the scheduler and include the information already collected.
- Weekly reporting: Rather than copying the same figures into a new spreadsheet every Friday, a workflow could assemble a draft report for someone to check.

In each case, the useful starting point is a clearly defined transfer or routine step. Customer advice, unusual requests, pricing decisions, and sensitive information still need appropriate human oversight.

Sometimes the best improvement is simpler than automation. If two spreadsheets serve the same purpose, you may be able to retire one. If a handoff keeps failing because nobody owns it, assigning responsibility may solve more than another notification would.

## Measure one process before changing it

Choose a task your team repeats often and track it for a normal working week. Record how many times it happens, how long it takes, and where someone has to correct or re-enter information. Ask the person doing the work what makes it frustrating.

Here is an illustrative calculation: a task that takes six minutes and happens ten times a day uses one hour daily, or five hours across a five-day week. That is the current workload, not five hours of guaranteed savings. Review, exceptions, and maintenance will still take time after a change.

Next, write down the steps and decide what a successful result would look like. Perhaps it is fewer duplicate records or a shorter wait between an inquiry and an assigned owner. Check whether your existing software can handle the routine step before adding another subscription.

Test with a small set of non-sensitive sample records. Include an incomplete form or a duplicate entry so you can see what happens when things are not perfect. Give someone responsibility for checking failures and keeping the process current.

Then compare the new process with your baseline. Count the time spent checking and fixing it, as well as the time saved. Keep what helps, adjust what does not, and expand only when the process is reliable.

## Start with the task you keep putting off

You do not need to redesign your entire business to identify a worthwhile improvement. Start with the repeated task that interrupts the day, holds up a colleague, or follows you home after closing.
